item.text: {"question_id":"8B.9","answer":"In the 2019–2023 period, López Obrador repeatedly used crises and institutional resistance to preserve his preferred governing direction, especially expanded military and executive control, but the supplied evidence shows mixed crisis-management effectiveness rather than reliable advancement of all objectives. The Culiacán operation ended with his direct order to release Ovidio Guzmán after federal forces were overmatched; the episode exposed weaknesses in intelligence, extraction planning, coordination, and territorial control, even though it avoided further reported civilian and military casualties (BATCH-0016-E004). His administration nevertheless consolidated militarization: it expanded the National Guard and other military roles, and the 2022 transfer of Guard control to Defense was implemented before the Supreme Court invalidated key control, command, and transitional provisions, with effects postponed until 2024 (BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0055-E006). The Ayotzinapa response began with a truth commission, a special prosecutor, independent experts, and formal cooperation commitments (BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0013-E001), but military non-disclosure, investigative interference, the departure of the expert group, and López Obrador’s continued defense of the Army left the investigation obstructed and delayed (BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0013-E003; BATCH-0030-E012). During Hurricane Otis, federal authorities deployed troops, established an air bridge, restored substantial infrastructure, and initiated reconstruction coordination, but aid distribution began slowly and unevenly, with poor residents reporting shortages and little assistance in the early aftermath (BATCH-0003-E022; BATCH-0031-E003; BATCH-0050-E010). In electoral resistance, López Obrador pursued Plan B to weaken the INE; mass opposition mobilized and the Supreme Court invalidated the reforms for legislative-procedure violations, after which governmental attacks continued (BATCH-0013-E016; BATCH-0014-E005). Internationally, Mexico advocated mediation and kept diplomatic channels open, but the evidence shows positioning and partner-supported coordination, not demonstrated influence over the conflicts (BATCH-0045-E012; BATCH-0012-E014; BATCH-0015-E015; BATCH-0015-E018). Overall, the evidence supports strong presidential agenda-setting and resilience in preserving regime priorities, but also recurring operational failures, institutional resistance, incomplete compliance, and limited proof that responses produced durable crisis resolution or broader stated objectives. Moral approval or disapproval of those objectives does not affect this execution assessment; moral effects belong in other chapters. Presidential attribution is strongest for strategic direction and formal decisions, while implementation and outcomes remain shared with military and civilian agencies, courts, subordinates, criminal
